title: Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz AI Productions Require Traditional Skills To Be Cinematic, Say Filmmakers On Kling AI Panel: “You Need Experts To Prevent Everything Looking The Same” Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions View All October 11, 2026 12:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ann Hui at the 31st Busan International Film Festival Busan International Film Festival Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui , who received the Camellia Award at the opening of Busan International Film Festival, shared her experiences of being a woman filmmaker in a male-dominated industry at a festival press conference, along with her thoughts on how Hong Kong cinema has evolved. When asked how other women had helped shape her career, Hui said she’d had five women bosses when she entered the industry back in the ‘70s who had welcomed her and helped her to become established as a filmmaker. “I was lucky because my first five bosses really supported me, gave me freedom and support, and allowed me to do what I wanted with the TV programs I was making. They were only criticizing me to make my work better,” Hui said. Related Stories News Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions News Netflix's 'The Blue Road' Director Han Jun-hee On Taking Risks With Stories & Shooting In Japan “Afterwards I met people who were not so nice, so I really want to talk about these five women in my masterclass. Some were company bosses and there were some actresses as well. It’s true that I seem to learn much less from men. I don’t know why because I’m not unfriendly with them, but perhaps it’s like karma in Buddhism, I don’t work with them as well.” Watch on Deadline Hui started her career working for Hong Kong broadcaster TVB, back then an incubator for Hong Kong’s new wave of pioneering filmmakers, before moving into features, many of which have won awards at major festivals, spanning the ‘80s to the present day. Her body of work includes an early trilogy about the Vietnamese boat people – Below The Lion Rock , The Story Of Woo Viet and Boat People – which was followed by films in a variety of genres including The Romance Of Book And Sword , Eighteen Springs , All About Love , A Simple Life , which won best actress in Venice, and The Golden Era, which won best director at Taiwan’s Golden Horse. Her most recent work, Elegies (2023), a documentary about Hong Kong poetry, opened Hong Kong International Film Festival and was nominated for the Golden Horse Awards. Looking back at developments in the Hong Kong film industry since the ‘70s, Hui also talked about the changing status of female filmmakers. “When I worked in TV in the ‘70s, and later when I made my first film, I tried my best to work on subjects like cops and robbers that men do,” Hui remembered. “I wanted to prove that women can do what men do.” “But once I’d fulfilled that intention, I got back to subjects that really interest me; about the predicament of people in modern-day society, which is also quite a lot about women. It wasn’t intentional to make women’s stories, that’s just the way it turned out.” She also observed that when she started her career, there were many women directors in television, but only two or three in the film industry. Now there are about 10-20 women directors actively working in the Hong Kong industry, she observed (including many that have had films screen in Busan, Hong Kong and Tokyo film festivals, including Norris Wong, Oliver Chan, Heiward Mak, Jessey Tsang and Cheuk Wan-chi). “Nowadays their position has become much better,” she continued. “Back in the ‘70s, I felt under pressure to have very masculine habits and dress like a man. It was almost like pretending to be a man when I’m on set. But nowadays, the female directors do not hide their gender when they’re working, and don’t mind coming across as quite feminine. They’re also much more conscious in the way they’re trying to make films telling women’s stories, which I think is totally legitimate.” While saying that she felt “very jealous” of developments in Korean cinema, Hui said she’s also encouraged by the new generation of Hong Kong filmmakers, who have a different approach to the freewheeling and commercially driven filmmakers of the ‘80s and ‘90s. “Despite the lack of investment, the young filmmakers in Hong Kong are still very dedicated, hardworking, and talented. I feel that if they have an opening, they will be able to make better films than we did, because in the ‘80s and ‘90s it was all about entertainment. There was a lot of volume but very little content. “But now the filmmakers are trying their best, perhaps because it’s so difficult to raise investment, they put a lot of effort into the planning and some of the films are really good.” She also mentioned the big improvements in acting in Hong Kong cinema. “Back in our era, most of the actors and actresses came from soap operas or beauty pageants. Now they all come from the Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts, so they have a really solid foundation in acting. They also have really professional ethics.” While accepting the Camellia Award at Busan’s opening ceremony, Hui mentioned that it was getting “more difficult” for her to make films as she turns eighty next year. She joked in the press conference about being worried that she’d trip on the red carpet because she’s not so steady on her feet these days. But she also said that she still enjoys making movies and is currently developing some ideas, so she’s not ready to announce her retirement just yet. “My judgment and understanding has not been reduced, in fact experience gives you a deeper understanding. So I still want to make films because I want to convey this new understanding that I have now in my work.” Jointly presented by BIFF and Chanel, the festival’s Camellia Award honors pioneering women filmmakers who advance the role of women in Asian cinema. title: Netflix Has Used AI on About 300 Titles, but “Human Touch Is Critical,” Exec Says in Busan
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All October 10, 2026 10:12pm From left: Film critic and moderator Yun Sung-eun; Sung Q Lee, Senior Director, APAC Production, Netflix; Kimball Thurston, CTO, Wētā FX; and director Kang Yun-sung Netflix Netflix has already used AI in various capacities on about 300 titles, one of its senior production executives said Saturday during an industry discussion at the Busan International Film Festival . Sung Q Lee, Netflix’s senior director of production for Asia-Pacific, said the technology was being deployed across the filmmaking process, but stressed the importance of preserving human creativity. “[AI] is being used in previsualization, production design, working out set-dressing concepts ahead of time, in editing and of course in VFX,” Lee said. “But the question that matters to me isn’t, ‘How much AI can we put into this title?’ but, ‘What more can this title do with AI’s help?’” Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay Sounds the Alarm Over the "Erosion of Democracy" at '14th' World Premiere: "We Need to Fight" Movies Oscars: U.K. Selects Iran Doc 'Rehearsals for a Revolution' as Best International Feature Entry Lee was speaking at Netflix’s annual Creative Asia event, presented in partnership with the Busan International Film Festival. The panel, co-hosted with the Motion Picture Association, also featured Korean filmmaker Kang Yun-sung, the director of The Outlaws and an enthusiastic adopter of AI tools, and Kimball Thurston, chief technology officer at Wētā FX. Much of the discussion focused on the opportunities AI could create for filmmakers working with limited budgets, although the speakers repeatedly emphasized the need to preserve human creative judgment. The occasion also highlighted just how differently the Hollywood creative community and Asian content sector tend to perceive the potential perils and promise of the technology, with the former profoundly wary and the latter seeing it mostly as an opportunity . Kang partnered with self-described AI filmmaker Kwon Han-seul last year to co-direct Run to the West , billed as Korea’s first fully AI-assisted feature. The project struggled at the box office amid bad buzz over its AI visuals, earning about $100,000. Kang said the pace of AI’s advancement meant the film already looked somewhat dated by the time of its release, but he remains undeterred about the technology’s potential for screen storytelling. The director is now in production on an action film called The Gulf of Aden , which heavily utilizes generative AI tools from China’s Kling AI. He said the technology has enabled him to realize myriad scenes that otherwise wouldn’t have been possible due to the budgetary constraints “that have held the Korean industry back from growing to its full potential.” Kang estimated that the AI-assisted approach could reduce the film’s production costs by around 40 percent. “When we calculated how much we’d save on The Gulf of Aden for financing, it came to a reduction of around 40 percent,” Kang said. “That’s not just from replacing CG and VFX. The shoot itself was streamlined, and that cut down our production time to some extent.” He added: “What has been buried due to budgetary issues was able to be put back on the table.” Netflix’s Sung tried to place AI within the context of the constant technological revolutions that have characterized the film industry since its earliest days. “Technological changes and new tools have helped a great deal with the ‘how,’ or how we make what we make better,” he said. “But they never decided the ‘why’ — why we have to tell this story.” “But when it comes to conveying emotion,” he later added, “ultimately, a human has to touch it. AI can get many jobs done, but does it touch human emotion? The human touch is critical and necessary.” Thurston similarly described Wētā FX’s use of the technology, so far, as “assistive AI,” rather than something that’s “allowed to change the creative intent in any way.” “It provides us — very fast — with the visual images and visualization. So from the director’s perspective or the cinematographer’s perspective, it’s very easy to identify the errors and correct them,” he explained. “Our goal is to reduce simple, repetitive tasks,” he added. title: ‘Saturday Night Live’: Shane Gillis’ Third Time Hosting Is Saved By Cast Newbie Grace Reiter
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Saturday Night Live’: Shane Gillis’ Third Time Hosting Is Saved By Cast Newbie Grace Reiter Shane Gillis Drops F-Bomb In ‘SNL’ “Green Eggs & Ham” Sketch, Apologizes Rohan Campbell Teases Directorial Debut Plans: “A Very Personal Story” View All October 10, 2026 10:06pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Grace Reiter and Shane Gillis on 'Saturday Night Live' NBC In his third time hosting Saturday Night Live , Shane Gillis isn’t making the case for a triumphant return to the cast. On this weekend’s episode, which also featured musical guest Rosalía, the comedian delivered several on-brand sketches that featured his signature everyman sense of humor, but no water cooler moments worth meme-ifying. Related Stories Late Night TV Shane Gillis Drops F-Bomb In ‘SNL’ “Green Eggs & Ham” Sketch Late Night TV ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution Gillis’ opening monologue was a tight five about his Bud Light commercials and getting into shape with workout buddies Joe Rogan and Theo Von, during which he put on his best femme voice to mimic gym gays and complained that “women just dress like whores now” at the gym. The comedian also noted that he’s “balded directly into an Adolph Hitler haircut,” and the only other option is looking gay. “That’s it, you’re either gay or Hitler. And isn’t that where we’re at as a country?” he quipped. Watch on Deadline In the first sketch, Gillis played the host of a cop talk show, in which he just arrested his various guests. Gillis then appeared in a country song music video, playing the father of a bride who imagines what he’ll do with her room when she moves out, only to end up hooking up with Ms. Pac-Man in a cloud of black mold. In a Green Eggs and Ham sketch, featuring Mikey Day as the Cat in the Hat and Gillis as his defensive son who thinks his dad is being scammed, the host made things interesting when he accidentally dropped an F-bomb . A History Channel sketch about WWII-time inventors patenting quiet shoes saw Gillis’ character finding them handy for “sneaking” around his wife, hence the name “sneakers.” Gillis also led a heating/AC commercial that’s honest about how much of a nightmare of a process is, complete with workers making fun of you, smoking in your doorway and staring through your windows. Meanwhile, new cast member Grace Reiter continued to prove her chops as she played problem child Coco in a “Weekend Update” segment in which her mom (Ashley Padilla) can’t find a babysitter. She was a perfect match for Padilla as the bratty daughter publicly embarrassing her mom. Reiter also shared a couple of sketches with Gillis, playing his elderly mother as a hospice nurse (Sarah Sherman) tells him she only has a few days, which conflicts with his plans to see Jelly Roll in Vegas. The sketch also features a cameo from Ben Marshall as Jelly Roll, Marcello Hernandez as Jesus and Rosalía as a horny divorcee, egging him on to make the concert. The final sketch of the episode was set in a kid’s chess tournament, where young TJ (Jeremy Culhane) tries to ignore his parents (Gillis and Reiter) in the stands, where they go from arguing exes to inappropriate flirtation. Saving the best for last, Reiter was certainly a bright spot on an otherwise dull episode. Gillis’ latest hosting gig on SNL comes after he hosted in 2024 and 2025 , following his removal from the NBC sketch comedy ‘s featured cast days after he was announced . title: ‘New Girl’ Stars Reunite — in a Slightly Different Way Than Max Greenfield Claimed
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All October 10, 2026 9:40pm Jake Johnson, Zooey Deschanel, Hannah Simone, Lamorne Morris, Max Greenfield and Damon Wayans Jr. attend the 2026 Chrysalis Butterfly Ball on Oct. 10 in Los Angeles. Monica Schipper/Getty Images Zooey Deschanel , Max Greenfield , Jake Johnson , Lamorne Morris , Hannah Simone and Damon Wayans Jr. had a New Girl reunion on Saturday night — in a different way than fans may have imagined. The stars came together at the Chrysalis Butterfly Ball in Los Angeles, where together they received the Rising Phoenix Award and Greenfield served as the evening’s host. The event was put on in support of Southern California nonprofit Chrysalis, which helps individuals navigate obstacles on their path to meaningful employment. The group’s night out came on the heels of a renewed push for an on-screen New Girl reunion, fueled by Greenfield fibbing in a Today appearance that creator Liz Meriwether had written “amazing” scripts for a revival. This set off a series of jokes between Meriwether and the cast, along with confirmation that there are no real plans for a reunion at this time. Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay Sounds the Alarm Over the "Erosion of Democracy" at '14th' World Premiere: "We Need to Fight" Lifestyle See Inside Jake Johnson's Pasadena Home (With Creative Studio) as Actor Lists Property for $3.29M Greenfield’s viral moment was a hot topic of conversation at the event, as Deschanel teased while the group accepted their award, “We especially would like to thank Max, who while organizing this announced that an actual New Girl reunion was happening and he made our lives so very annoying.” “Now is probably not the most appropriate time to apologize for this but yes, that’s something that happened and I am sorry. It did, however, bring a lot of attention to Chrysalis and what we are doing here tonight, accidentally,” Greenfield responded. “When the six of us reunite — six actors, none of whom graduated college except apparently Hannah, which does make a lot of sense; Jake says he did graduate college, which no one believes — but when we come together, remarkably people pay attention and people show up, and we are so grateful that you showed up tonight.” Jake Johnson, Zooey Deschanel, Hannah Simone, Lamorne Morris, Max Greenfield and Damon Wayans Jr. have a #NewGirl reunion at the Chrysalis Butterfly Ball charity event pic.twitter.com/ZLMyOyuMrU — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) October 11, 2026 On the carpet, Greenfield, who organized the big moment via the stars’ group chat, teased to The Hollywood Reporter that instead of making such a public declaration on national television, “I probably should have just said there is a New Girl reunion and it’s happening on Oct. 10 in support of Chrysalis. I got excited and then we found an opportunity for a fun pivot and said, ‘Actually, it’s this.'” Johnson, though, wasn’t letting him off the hook that easily, declaring, “He did such a bad job it was unbelievable.” The actor noted how he and Morris play a game where they “talk shit to each other via interviews — Max didn’t get the memo and sincerely said he read scripts and they were great, with no joke or insult. Then Liz had to step in and say, ‘My lawyer wrote me, you idiot.’ So that is Max being Max,” teasing, “there was zero strategy. He texted me after and said, ‘I think I did a bad job.’ And he did.” The Butterfly Ball — held at The Beehive — also honored Jared Wolff, chairman and CEO of Banc of California, with the Corporate Trailblazer Award; Guadalupe Rios, a former Chrysalis participant and current Caltrans employee, received the John Dillon Award. title: ‘SNL’: Shane Gillis Shares “Gas Station Egg” Nickname From Joe Rogan, Pete Hegseth Celebrates USS Lincoln San Diego Homecoming

Logo text Shane Gillis returned for his third Saturday Night Live hosting stint, where he revealed the nickname Joe Rogan and Theo Von came up for him (“gas station egg”) and his gripes with his “Adolf Hitler haircut.” The comedian started his monologue by talking about how he wanted to lose weight: “I gotta lose weight. It’s a bummer, you know what I mean? When you finally get so fat, you’re like, alright, hit that fat rock bottom.” Gillis shared a story about how hiking wasn’t for him, and then explained his contention with public gyms. “Going to the public gym as a fat guy, especially in New York, is a nightmare, dude. It’s just the hottest gay guys you’ve ever seen. They’re jacked and they look at me, like, ‘Yeah, right.’ ‘I know, dude,’” he said. TV 'SNL UK' Season 2: All the Hosts and Musical Guests “Also, I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now,” Gillis said. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial vape-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look!” Gillis then raved about Rogan’s own gym that is equipped with a sauna. I look over and it was Theo Von and Joe, and they opened the door, and Joe just goes, ‘Hey, Theo said you looked like a gas station egg.'” “The thing that hurt the most was when he closed the glass door, I saw my own reflection and I looked exactly like a gas station egg,” he added. “That’s one of the meanest things anyone’s told me: ‘You look like a wet, bagged, hard boiled egg.'” Gillis said he was used to receiving insults growing up having two older sisters, who he called “big, fat-bitch sisters.” He went on to note that “the thing that I’m really bothered by is I’ve balded directly into an Adolf Hitler haircut.” He added, “And it’s not good, because I give a lot of speeches and the front falls down a lot, and there’s no way to adjust it without looking exactly like [Hitler]. It’s the only way. I’m not going to [move it], that’s gay. That’s it: You’re either gay or you’re Hitler, and isn’t that where we’re at as a country?” Later in the episode, Gillis accidentally said the F-word live on-air during a Dr. Seuss sketch where his character was stressing that his father didn’t want to eat green eggs and ham. “Bro, it’s a non-starter. title: ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution

title: ‘Treasure Island’ Review: David Oyelowo and Hayley Atwell Can Only Breathe So Much Life Into MGM+’s Handsome but Undercooked Pirate Adventure
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All October 10, 2026 8:40pm 'Treasure Island' Cris Rios Bordon/Playground Entertainment/Paramount Global You cannot fault Treasure Island , MGM+’s new take on the Robert Louis Stevenson classic, for a lack of effort. Where some adaptations of beloved literary works might be content to recreate the source material beat for beat, creator Robert Murphy reimagines it wholesale. Characters and plot elements are mixed and matched with abandon. Themes of subjugation and rebellion are brought to the forefront, while real historical events like the Haitian Revolution play out in the background. Treasure Island The Bottom Line Admirably ambitious, disappointingly flat. Airdate: Sunday, Oct. 11 (MGM+) Cast: Tom Sweet, David Oyelowo, Hayley Atwell, Jack Huston, Tomer Capote, Tristan Sturrock, Craige Els, Neil Pendleton, Mayen Mehta, George Frost, Tadghe Murphy Creator: Robert Murphy The main cast is strong ( David Oyelowo , playing the famed pirate Long John Silver, proves particularly adept at doing a lot with a little) and the detailed settings appealingly solid. In its intention to dazzle you with swashbuckling thrills in the moment, and leave you with deeper ideas to chew on in the aftermath, Treasure Island shows admirable ambition. It’s the execution, flat and repetitive and ultimately rather dreary, that lets it down. Related Stories Movies 'The Basics of Philosophy' Review: Paul Schrader Does Some Deep -- and Discomfiting -- Thinking About a College Professor's Guilt Movies Paul Schrader Says He Can't Stop Writing About Guilt: "You Don't Outrun Your Childhood" It takes a while to reveal its shortcomings, however. Initially, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. Our hero to come of age is Jim Hawkins (Tom Sweet), a sweet-natured fellow with the height of a man, the acne-spotted cheeks of a teenager, the wide-eyed innocence of a boy and, most importantly to the plot, the eidetic memory of almost no one of any age. Jim and his widowed mother, Bess ( Hayley Atwell ), are barely scraping by running a bustling tavern, even with the occasional extra coin they pull in by having drunkards bet on Jim’s gift for perfect recall. Then hopes of a better life suddenly wash up ashore in the form of Billy Bones ( The Boys ’ Tomer Capone ), a shipwrecked pirate telling a wild tale of buried treasure and toting the cryptic map to prove it. Unfortunately for Billy but fortunately, in theory, for Treasure Island ’s ability to craft a rip-roaring adventure, he’s not the only one after this legendary trove. As Jim and Bess race to the Caribbean on a ship chartered by a wealthy merchant, Graham ( Jack Huston ), they find themselves unwelcomely accompanied by Long John Silver, who was none too pleased when his former crewmate Billy absconded with that map. The first few of Treasure Island ‘s six hour-long chapters manage to stay afloat thanks to some helpful assets. One is that it is generally quite handsome, in a polished if not especially inventive way. From baroque European manors to endless blue seas to overgrown jungles, the world looks expansive and lived-in — no small thing at a time when big series like this so often look overrun with green screen. It’s easy to want to keep looking at this show. More crucially, it benefits from a few performers capable of popping through the screen on sheer power of their charisma. The most compelling figure is Long John Silver, whose every glare or sneer or smirk Oyelowo imbues with a whole spectrum of feeling — the fury of a formerly enslaved man who’s had to fight tooth and nail for every scrap he’s ever gotten, the icy calculation of one clever and tough enough to have won all those battles, the flashes of decency still buried somewhere deep within. The most fun is Bess, a scheming single mom whose ability to manipulate lovelorn men is akin to a superpower. Atwell makes her slyly funny and unapologetically mercenary — I laughed at how little she bothers to hide her delight when Huston’s Graham speaks of being lonely after his wife’s passing — and she’s never more appealing than when she’s paired with Capone, who gives off his own louche pan-Continental sex appeal. When they’re talking low and close, Treasure Island flirts with transitioning, incongruously but amusingly, into an overheated bodice-ripper. Atwell and Oyelowo are working so hard, in fact, that it’s initially easy to overlook how thin the writing really is. The dynamics between the characters are complicated in the sense that they’re nearly all informed by ulterior motives and mutable loyalties. Everyone’s forever making false promises, or planning mutinies, or framing one another for murder, such that keeping up with their crisscrossing alliances becomes a head-spinning challenge. Emotionally, however, the experience feels empty, not least because most of these characters are defined and driven only by their desire for gold. You might as well be watching computers outwit each other at chess. Once again, the flatness does not entirely seem to be for lack of trying. Treasure Island likes and understands Bess well enough to give her a chance to explain that, as a woman in a man’s world, “I am all I have to trade” — can you blame her for deploying her feminine wiles to get ahead? It’s curious enough about Silver to grant Oyelowo a brief but bitter monologue recounting his youth spent in bondage, and all the horrors he endured therein — the pirate-infested seas may be “no place for an honest man,” but doesn’t it contain a few antiheroes worth rooting for anyway? But then, having raised these ideas, Treasure Island simply leaves them hanging in the air, unconnected to much of anything else. They’re serious but simplistic motivations, and ones all the harder to trust because when everyone is so duplicitous it’s nearly impossible to tell if anyone means anything they’re saying. Even the one clearly earnest bond in the ensemble, between Bess and Jim, lacks a meaningful sense of history or nuance — I couldn’t begin to guess how such a cunning woman raised such a naïve kid, or what lessons he’s learned or rejected under her guidance. While it doesn’t help that young Sweet is outmatched by his more experienced costars, it’s hard to place the blame on him when there’s such scant evidence of depth anywhere else either. When the parent-child bond is fractured, the show barely bothers to give Jim a moment of reflection or regret before it simply barrels ahead to the next plot point. In the series’ defense, those plot points involve objectively exciting things like an armed revolution, an aristocratic dinner party, a trek through the jungle, an active volcano and more guns held to temples and knives held to throats than any human could reasonably be expected to keep track of. (Not much graphic violence, though, give or take an upsetting shot of a murdered cat.) You can see why Jim and his companions would want to rush headlong toward them. It’s just that in the absence of any reason to care all that much about the fates of these characters, even a raucous bar fight or a daring escape turns out to be a slog. If it’s a cliché that the real treasure is the friends we made along the way, it’s one Treasure Island proves true via the negative: Without anyone to feel for, even the most glittering cache of ill-gotten jewels might be rendered dull and mundane. THR

title: Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz AI Productions Require Traditional Skills To Be Cinematic, Say Filmmakers On Kling AI Panel: “You Need Experts To Prevent Everything Looking The Same” Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions View All October 10, 2026 7:18pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source SFA Executive Director Stepan Burnashev & PGK President Lee Dong-ha Sakha Filmmakers Association EXCLUSIVE: The Producers Guild of Korea (PGK) and the Sakha Filmmakers Association (SFA) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) aimed at creating a direct route to international co-productions and professional exchange between the Korean and Sakha screen production sectors. The Sakha Republic (Yakutia), in Russia’s Far East, has built one of the country’s most procative film industries, making films mostly in the Sakha (Yakut) language and developing a strong local theatrical audience. Its films have been drawing growing attention at festivals and markets across Asia and internationally. Related Stories News Netflix's 'The Blue Road' Director Han Jun-hee On Taking Risks With Stories & Shooting In Japan News AI Tools Bring Efficiencies But Have Limitations, Says Weta CTO Kimball Thurston: "Tech Companies Should Collaborate More With Creatives" The MOU with PGK was signed at the Sakha Filmmakers Association booth during the Asian Contents & Film Market ( ACFM ) in Busan , with the aim of starting a long-term industry partnership between producers from the two territories. Watch on Deadline Under the agreement, PGK and SFA will establish a new framework for co-production between Korean and Sakha producers, aimed at developing projects together and sharing information on public financing available in both territories. The partnership will include project showcases, producer-to-producer meetings and B2B sessions designed to identify projects with international potential and move them towards co-production. The two organisations will also bring the partnership to major international markets, including ACFM, Hong Kong Filmart and the Cannes Marché du Film, creating new opportunities for Sakha projects to connect with the wider Asian and international industry. For PGK, the agreement continues a programme of international partnerships built since the pandemic, alongside MOUs with the Canadian Media Producers Association (CMPA), the Hong Kong Film Production Executives Association (HKFPEA), the Indonesian Film Producers Association (APROFI) and the Brazilian Audiovisual Industry Union (SIAESP). PGK President Lee Dong-ha said: “Sakha cinema is one of the most distinctive voices to emerge in Asia in recent years, and it belongs in the conversation among Asian producers. Through this MOU, PGK and SFA open a direct channel between our two production communities – one that we intend to turn into actual co-productions.” Stepan Burnashev, SFA’s Executive Director, said: “Sakha cinema grew from a small regional community into a strong local film culture because our filmmakers kept telling stories in our own language and from our own perspective. “Korea is an important example of how a strong local identity can connect with audiences around the world. This agreement gives our producers a direct working relationship with the Korean industry. We want it to lead not only to exchange, but to projects developed and produced together, and to a lasting connection between our filmmaking communities.” ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie & Bacall Read More About: Comments

title: DOJ Launches Investigation Of Networks For Suspending TV Pool Amid Trump’s Ban On CNN
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution DOJ Launches Investigation Of Networks For Suspending TV Pool Amid Trump’s Ban On CNN Donald Trump Picks Katie Zacharia As Next White House Press Secretary View All October 10, 2026 6:05pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet President of China Xi Jinping and first lady of China Peng Liyuan. Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images UPDATED: The Justice Department has launched an investigation into whether the five major networks violated antitrust laws when they suspended participation in the White House TV pool in protest of Donald Trump ‘s ban on CNN . Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the Justice Department, said in a statement, “Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.” The New York Times first reported on the investigation. Related Stories News Donald Trump Picks Katie Zacharia As Next White House Press Secretary News FCC Chairman Declines To Say Whether Broadcast Outlets Should Be Allowed To Air Live Execution, But It's Doubtful Networks Would Show It Anyway After Trump announced his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds on Sept. 18, CNN also was restricted from the TV pool. As part of a long-running arrangement, CNN, CBS News , ABC News , NBC News and Fox News rotate pool duty providing technical, video and reporting coverage of the president, with feeds then distributed to other networks and news organizations. The pool is necessary because of the space limitations of areas of the White House, like the Oval Office, or on Air Force One. Watch on Deadline After the CNN freeze out, the other members of the TV pool jointly announced on Sept. 21 that they would refrain from their rotation turn, a move made to protest the White House effort to block the news network. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” the five networks said in a statement at the time. The suspension lasted for about four days, but it came during the White House visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping. The suspension of the TV pool meant that there was much less video coverage of major ceremonies and other events surrounding his visit. Trump later complained that CNN and MS NOW did not cover Xi’s visit, without mentioning his efforts to ban the two outlets from the White House grounds. ABC confirmed that it has not received any notification of the investigation but it expects to. A CNN spokesperson declined to comment. Other networks in the pool did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The White House has continued to restrict CNN from certain assignments, including flying on Air Force One on presidential trip. After Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from White House grounds, those three media outlets sued, claiming violations of their First Amendment and due process rights. A federal judge imposed a temporary restraining order, which last until Tuesday, that has forced the White House to renew access to dozens of reporters. The judge, Timothy Kelly, is expected to rule by then on whether to grant the news outlets a preliminary injunction, something that would prevent the White House from denying access on a longer term. The issue of access to the White House grounds is separate, yet related, to the issue of whether the administration can also freeze out members of the pool because the president does not approve of their editorial decisions. A different case, involving the Associated Press, is on appeal in the D.C. Circuit. The AP was barred from the White House pool because its style guidance did not adhere to Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The investigation has the potential to set up another legal battle against the Trump administration over the First Amendment. Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for the Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the investigation “appears to be a pretext for seeking records from the networks about how they are covering daily White House events during a media ban the president himself put in place. The decisions news organizations make about coverage are protected by the First Amendment, and summoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.” Seth Stern, chief of advocacy for Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement, “The investigation is nonsense. Trump may view the presidency as a business venture, but news outlets’ standing up for their constitutional rights has nothing to do with antitrust law, no matter what Laura Loomer says.” Loomer is the conspiracy theorist and Trump loyalist who posted last month about using antitrust law to punish the networks. The administration has been rebuffed in the federal courts in another effort to seek materials from media organizations as part of an antitrust investigation. Last year, a federal judge barred the Federal Trade Commission from issuing a civil investigative demand to Media Matters for America, the progressive watchdog group, as part of an antitrust investigation of an advertiser boycott of Elon Musk’s X. Media Matters later said that a settlement with the FTC required that the agency forgo issuing such a civil investigation demand. They also said that the “agreement — and the decisions Media Matters won in the district court and the court of appeals — offers a roadmap for other newsgathering and nonprofit organizations facing, or at risk of, government retaliation.” Three advertising holding companies, WPP, Dentsu and Publicis, also reached a settlement with the FTC. A legal battle also would be a test for David Ellison, the CEO of Skydance, which completed its merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. this past week. The Justice Department’s Antitrust Division gave the greenlight to the transaction in June. Vowing to protect editorial independence, Ellison said at a town hall that he backed CNN’s lawsuit over the ban on White House access. ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set Laika’s Stop-Motion Epic ‘Wildwood’; Brad Bird’s Sci-Fi Noir ‘Ray Gunn’ Read More About: 12 Comments

title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Drops New Trailer, Team Teases a Detective Story Set When Replicants Take Over
full_text: Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All October 10, 2026 5:47pm Blade Runner 2099 Amazon MGM Studios Logo text Prime Video released a new Blade Runner 2099 trailer during the upcoming series’ New York Comic Con panel on Saturday. Michelle Yeoh , Hunter Schafer , Dimitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Matthew Needham, showrunner Silka Luisa, and executive producers Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson appeared on the Saturday evening panel, where the cast and creative team teased what’s in store for fans of the franchise and how the series will be different than its film installments. At the core of the show is a mystery surrounding Olwen, a replicant Blade Runner who is “supposed to be looking for human insurgents, humans that continue to fight back,” said Luisa. “But… she’s actually here looking for a Blade Runner who’s gone missing, Merrick, one of her colleagues, and that’s the first time that happened,” she teased. Related Stories TV 'Star Trek: Starfleet Academy' Season 2 to Premiere March 2027, Bill Nighy and Rosemarie DeWitt to Guest Star TV Nicolas Cage Teases 'True Detective' Role, Says He "Probably" Won't Work With Prime Video Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for 'Spider-Noir' Speaking to her human character, Schafer shared she is “more or less a fugitive in hiding from LAPD Blade Runners. Her work gets raided, and she’s gotta go on the run and make sure she protects her little brother, and ultimately undergo this mission where she goes undercover as a Blade Runner with LAPD.” Yeoh teased that her character is dying in the limited series: “She knows the time is running out, and she’s a character that doesn’t like to leave things unfinished.” During a clip shown exclusively to the room, Yeoh’s character can be seen with blue-like nail beds, which Luisa explained was inspired by the original Blade Runner film and indicates Yeoh’s character is dying. “It was something early on where we wanted to have a visual signifier… to never forget that she’s dying. She’s so powerful. She’s still so vital, and so there needed to be some marker that she could always look down and remember it’s only days,” she said. “We look to the first film as a reference for how to do it. In that, with Roy Batty, there’s a couple of really, really gnarly shots where you see his hands and his nails, and it makes sense. It’s an extremity, so maybe his heart is shifting, and it’s harder to pump blood there. But we thought that was going to be a really clever way to see the progression over the season as she gets closer to death.” According to the showrunner, Blade Runner 2099 answers what happens when our time as a species ends. “We are 50 years after 2049 , and bad news. The worst has happened. The replicant uprising that has been bubbling up in the films has taken place, and humans have lost,” she teased. “ 2099 is taking place at a junction point when one species is ending and a new one is rising. The first film, something I loved about it was that it was looking at mortality on a micro level. Roy Batty and the other replicants were fighting for more life. This show asked that same question, but on a macro level. Mankind, what happens when we realize our time is running out? Are we going to accept that loss? Can we hold on to our humanity during it?” During the panel, the EPs teased that the limited series will explore how humans and replicants are also both searching for identity. For humans, it’s about finding their identity in a world in which they’re no longer the dominant species, and for replicants, it’s trying to find their identity in a world where they are the dominant species and what that future looks like. “The show is really about a birth,” Luisa continued later on in the panel. “It’s about the birth of a city, of a society, of our characters, and it’s really the dawn of this new era. And in terms of that, when I think of a birth, I think it’s hot, sticky, bright, chaotic, and that’s where the environment came from.” Speaking to how the show’s aesthetic expands upon the films, the showrunner noted that “the first original film actually has a very different aesthetic than 2049, and so 2099 needed to have a third aesthetic. It needed to honor what came before it, but it needed to also introduce audiences to something original [that] still felt foreign.” She later explained how key production design was to delivering that. “So many of the sets are 360. The lighting is built into them. There are monitors with graphics that background actors are interacting with. There are mechanical elements that are moving. It really feels like a functional environment, and it’s a fake world,” she told the NYCC crowd. “It’s not just the creation; it’s also the aging, the weathering, the layering. There are bobbleheads on top of the desks and soda cans that have been left. You really get a sense that people are living here and they’re working here.” In terms of why EP Johnson signed on to this vision of Blade Runner, he pointed to a saying about science fiction. “Great science fiction isn’t actually about the future; it’s about the present. When Silka first came to see us now several years ago, the idea of something replacing humans at the top of the food chain, as it were, and what happens with humanity at that point seemed very resonant to us,” he shared. “Sitting here this evening in October of 2026, as we’re all living in a world with the emergence of artificial intelligence, what does that mean for our future? We’ll let all of you decide about the show, of course. But we think that the themes of the show and the dilemmas for the characters are very relatable.” Added Kosove, it was an “interesting and clever” departure from the existing world of Blade Runner . “It’s someone going undercover, and that dynamic between a human pretending to be a replicant and Owen, whose time is running out, and the impact that they have on one another is at the core of what the show is about,” he said. “I also think, just from the standpoint of a mystery where you’re peeling back the onion and going back and having clues and Easter eggs through both movies — even before the first movie — I thought was a tremendous, exciting thing to explore.” The series offers a completely different spin, according to Yeoh. “We all love the original, but now to go 50 years forward, things have changed tremendously.” For Needham, it’s an exciting thriller and “a great detective story. There is a really exciting, beautiful mystery at the heart of it, and there’s also this huge philosophical debate going on around it that is about being human, and all the mysteries involved in that tied up.” Speaking to what the audience can expect from the mystery of the series, Luisa told the NYCC crowd that the story will be about how “replicants are in control” but don’t have full humanity. “They have agency, but they are made in our likeness. So they still have desires, and they still want more than what they’ve been given. You can’t see much of it, but in that clip, it’s actually the red light district. Instead of selling sex, it sells experiences, human experience,” the showrunner said. “Replicants still can’t get pregnant. They can’t get old. They still want more than what they’ve been given, and they see all these humans out there, and they have they have a life that they still can’t have.” She concluded: “The mystery is asking why Merrick, someone who fought and sacrificed for all this power, is now turning his back and walking away from it. And the question is for what?” THR
